title: The Heaven and Earth Society
bigQuestion: How can we tell a society's proud founding legend from what the records show, and why do both matter?

story.title: A Sign at the Tea Stall
story.kicker: Far from home and out of money, a young man remembers the sign his sworn brothers taught him.
paragraphs: It is around the year 1800 in southern China. A young man stands at a busy river landing. Months ago he left his family's village in Fujian to look for work. He has carried loads on his back and slept wherever he could. Now his money is gone. The town around him is loud and full of strangers. He is a composite, based on the kinds of men historians have found in old records.

Back home, an older man had brought him into a brotherhood. Its members called it the Heaven and Earth Society. They swore an oath to treat each other as brothers. They taught him a few secret signs and a line of verse. "If you are ever in trouble far from home," the older man had said, "use them."

At a tea stall by the landing, the young man sits down. He sets his cup and his hands in a careful way, just as he was taught. Most people would not notice anything. But a man at the next table looks up. He asks a question that sounds ordinary. The young man answers with the line of verse he memorized. The stranger smiles.

Within an hour, the young man is eating a bowl of rice in a back room with three new brothers. One knows of a job loading boats. Another offers a mat to sleep on. They are poor too, but they share what they have. For a man alone in a strange town, this brotherhood can mean the difference between hunger and a meal.

This chapter tells the story of that brotherhood. It began as a way for poor, traveling men to help each other. Later it grew a heroic legend, spread across the world and split into many groups. Some did great good. Some turned to crime. Learning to tell these strands apart is the work of this chapter.
story.think: What does a person need most when they are far from home? How could a secret sign help meet that need?

lessons.title: China in the 1700s
lessons.mainIdea: In the 1700s, China's population grew fast, and many poor men left home to find work.
reading: In the 1700s, China was ruled by the Qing dynasty. A *dynasty* is a line of rulers from one family. The Qing emperors came from the Manchu people of the northeast. They ruled China from 1644 until 1912. The 1700s were a time of peace and growth under strong emperors such as Qianlong.

During that century, China's population grew very quickly. There was not enough good farmland for every family. Many young men left their villages to find work. They became peddlers, boatmen, porters and laborers. A *migrant* is a person who moves from one place to another to find work or a better life.

Life on the road was hard and lonely. A migrant in a strange town had no family nearby. If he got sick, lost his job or was robbed, he might have no one to turn to. In southern provinces such as Fujian, on China's southeast coast, many men faced this problem. Some decided to make new families of their own, bound by promises.

words.d: a line of rulers who come from the same family
a person who moves from one place to another to find work or a better life

lessons.title: Sworn Brothers in Fujian
lessons.mainIdea: Qing records show the Heaven and Earth Society began around 1761 or 1762 in Fujian as a brotherhood for mutual aid.
reading: Around 1761 or 1762, men gathered at a small Buddhist pavilion in the township of Gaoxi, in Zhangpu county, Fujian. The pavilion honored Guanyin, a figure of mercy in Chinese Buddhism. A monk called Wan Tixi, also known as Tixi, was linked to the founding. Their group became known as the Tiandihui, which means the Heaven and Earth Society.

The members were bound by an *oath*, a solemn promise made before witnesses. They promised to treat each other as brothers. This is called a *sworn brotherhood*. Sworn brotherhood was an old custom in China. The famous novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms tells of three heroes who swore to be brothers in a peach garden.

Why join? The historian Dian Murray, working with the Chinese scholar Qin Baoqi, studied Qing government records. Their 1994 book argues that the society began as a *mutual aid* brotherhood. Mutual aid means members help each other with money, shelter, protection and support in hard times. In their view, politics came later.

words.d: a solemn promise made before witnesses
a group of people who promise by oath to treat each other as brothers
members of a group helping each other with money, shelter, protection and support

look.title: What the Historians Found

look.cite: Dian H. Murray with Qin Baoqi, The Origins of the Tiandihui: The Chinese Triads in Legend and History (Stanford University Press, 1994)

lessons.title: Help for Men on the Move
lessons.mainIdea: The society gave poor, traveling men protection and a network of help far from home.
reading: Picture a peddler walking from town to town with his goods hanging from a pole. Roads could be dangerous. Bandits robbed travelers. Local bullies pushed newcomers around. A man alone had little protection. A man with sworn brothers in the next town had help waiting.

The historian David Ownby studied brotherhoods like this in his 1996 book on early and mid-Qing China. He and Murray found that members were mostly poor, mobile men: peddlers, boatmen, laborers and others far from their families. The society gave them a *network*, a set of people linked together who can help one another.

Was the society a rebel group from the start? This question is still debated. Murray, Qin and Ownby argue that it began mainly for mutual aid and protection. In their view, slogans against the Qing grew later and varied from group to group. Other writers, especially after 1900, described it as *revolutionary* from its very first day, meaning it aimed to overthrow the government.

words.d: a set of people linked together who can help one another
aiming to overthrow a government and replace it with a new one

lessons.title: How Brothers Knew Each Other
lessons.mainIdea: Members recognized each other with hand signs, lines of verse and ways of arranging teacups.
reading: Members of the society lived in many towns, and most had never met. So how could a stranger prove he was a brother? The society used *recognition signs*. These were secret ways of showing membership that outsiders would not notice. They worked like a password you could say with your hands.

Sources from the 1800s describe several kinds of signs. Members held their fingers in certain positions. They arranged teacups on a table in special patterns. They recited lines of poetry. They also used *split characters*. A split character is a Chinese written character broken into pieces, so only insiders could read the hidden word.

Some care is needed with this evidence. Most of what we know comes from papers that police seized, or from outsiders who studied them. Historians are not sure how often ordinary members really used these signs in daily life. This course describes the kinds of signs but does not teach real ones.

words.d: secret ways for members to show each other who they are without outsiders noticing
Chinese written characters broken into pieces so that only insiders could read them

look.cite: National Museum of Singapore, William Stirling Collection, "Stirling's notes on forms of recognition used by triad societies" (accession 1996-02885-038)

lessons.title: The Interpreter in Batavia
lessons.mainIdea: Gustaaf Schlegel's 1866 book translated seized society papers, making it both scholarship and a tool for police.
reading: In the 1860s, the island of Java was ruled by the Netherlands. Its main city, Batavia, is today's Jakarta, in Indonesia. Many Chinese migrants lived there. A young Dutch *interpreter* named Gustaaf Schlegel worked for the colonial government. An interpreter translates between languages. Schlegel worked from society papers that Dutch colonial police had seized.

Schlegel translated the papers into English. He published them in 1866 as Thian Ti Hwui: The Hung-League or Heaven-Earth-League. The book shows membership certificates, oaths, flags, poems and signs, with folded plates of drawings. It was the first full study of the society by a Western scholar.

The book has two sides. It preserved documents that might otherwise have been lost. It also helped *colonial* governments, Dutch and British, watch and police the society. Members saw a sworn brotherhood with a proud history. Colonial officials saw a network of rebels and criminals. Both views sit inside Schlegel's pages.

words.d: a person who translates between languages
having to do with a country that rules another people's land

lessons.title: Outsiders See Themselves
lessons.mainIdea: Western writers often compared the society to Freemasonry, but historians find no shared origin.
reading: In the 1800s and early 1900s, some British and Dutch writers who studied the society were Freemasons. *Freemasons* are members of a brotherhood that began in Europe, with its own signs, oaths and lodges. When these writers read about Chinese hand signs and oaths, they saw something familiar. Some called the society Chinese Freemasonry.

In 1925 and 1926, J. S. M. Ward and W. G. Stirling published a three-volume study called The Hung Society. It compared the society's rituals with Masonic ones. Historians today find books like this useful as records. They also warn that such writers over-read the links between the two traditions.

This shows a common pattern. When people meet something new, they compare it to what they already know. That can help, but it can also mislead. A shared feature is a *parallel*, not proof of a shared origin. The Heaven and Earth Society grew from Chinese customs of sworn brotherhood, not from European lodges.

words.d: members of a brotherhood that began in Europe, with its own signs, oaths and lodges
a feature two things share, which does not prove they came from the same source

lessons.title: The Legend of the Shaolin Monks
lessons.mainIdea: The society's founding legend tells of loyal Shaolin monks betrayed by the Qing.
reading: Members of the society learned a founding story. In it, monks of the Shaolin Temple help the Kangxi emperor defeat his enemies in the 1670s. Instead of rewarding them, officials betray them and burn their temple. Only five monks escape. They become the Five Ancestors, and they found the brotherhood.

In the legend, the survivors swear to overthrow the Qing and restore the *Ming*. The Ming was the Chinese dynasty that the Qing had replaced in 1644. The story gave members a noble past. It made their brotherhood part of a heroic fight for loyalty and justice. It also gave them a shared enemy.

A *legend* is a traditional story about the past that may not be true, but that people value. A founding legend explains where a group came from and what it stands for. Legends matter even when they are not accurate. They tell us what members believed about themselves and hoped to be.

words.d: the Chinese dynasty that ruled before the Qing took power in 1644
a traditional story about the past that may not be true, but that people value

look.prompt: What does each story say about the values of the group that tells it? Why might people keep telling a story even if no records prove it?

lessons.title: What the Qing Files Show
lessons.mainIdea: Qing officials investigated the society after an uprising in Taiwan, and their records point to a founding around 1761.
reading: The Qing government first took serious notice of the society in Taiwan in the 1780s. A cloth peddler from Fujian named Yan Yan had brought the brotherhood across the sea. In 1786, officials banned the society and arrested members, including uncles of a local leader named Lin Shuangwen. In 1787, Lin and his followers rose up against the government.

The *uprising*, an armed revolt against a government, lasted into 1788. The Qianlong emperor sent a large army to crush it. He later celebrated the victory with a set of engravings showing the campaign. Then his officials asked a hard question: where did this society come from? They questioned arrested members and followed the trail back to Fujian.

The questioning produced *confessions*, statements in which arrested people admitted what they knew or did. These records are kept today in archives in Beijing and Taipei. Historians Dian Murray and Qin Baoqi studied them. They found no evidence of the society before about 1761. The Shaolin story of the 1670s appears in no record from that time.

words.d: an armed revolt against a government
statements in which arrested people admit what they knew or did

lessons.title: Weighing the Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Both legends and government records are evidence, but each has limits a historian must weigh.
reading: Historians sort sources into kinds. A *primary source* is made at the time by people involved, such as a letter, a diary or a government report. A secondary source is written later by someone studying the past. The Qing confessions are primary sources. Murray and Qin's book is a secondary source built on them.

Government records are strong evidence for dates, places and names. Officials wrote them close to the events. But they have limits. People questioned under arrest may say what officials want to hear, or hide what they know. Officials also had a *bias*. They saw the society as a danger, so they described it that way. A careful historian reads such records with those limits in mind.

The legend has limits too. No record from the 1670s mentions it. The goal of restoring the Ming does not appear in the society's own writings until around 1800. In the early 1900s, revolutionaries around Sun Yat-sen retold the legend to win support against the Qing. Still, the legend is real evidence of what members believed and valued. Weighing both kinds of sources gives the fullest picture.

words.d: something made at the time by people involved, such as a letter, diary or report
a leaning toward one view that can color how someone reports events

lessons.title: The Hongmen Spread Worldwide
lessons.mainIdea: As Chinese migrants moved overseas, Hongmen groups went with them and took many forms.
reading: The society went by many names. One of the most common was *Hongmen*, often put in English as the Hong League. As Chinese people moved abroad in the 1800s, to Southeast Asia, Hawaii, the Americas and beyond, many brought the brotherhood with them. Each new place shaped the groups in its own way.

Overseas, Hongmen groups did many jobs. They helped newcomers find work and housing. They settled quarrels, cared for the sick and made sure the dead were buried. In North America, one large branch was the Chee Kung Tong. In English it often called itself the Chinese Freemasons, though it had no link of origin with European Freemasonry.

Some Hongmen groups turned to politics. In 1904, in Honolulu, the revolutionary leader Sun Yat-sen joined the Hongmen. He hoped to win the support of overseas Chinese for a revolution against the Qing. In 1911 and 1912, the Qing dynasty fell. China became a *republic*, a country led by elected leaders instead of an emperor.

words.d: a common name for the Heaven and Earth Society and the many groups that grew from it
a country led by elected leaders instead of a king or emperor

lessons.title: When Some Branches Turned to Crime
lessons.mainIdea: Some groups descended from the Hongmen became criminal gangs called triads, but they are not the whole tradition.
reading: Not every branch kept to mutual aid. Over time, some groups that traced their roots to the Hongmen became criminal gangs. Outsiders came to call them *triads*. The name comes from a triangle symbol linked to heaven, earth and humanity. Triad gangs made money through crimes such as illegal gambling and *extortion*, which means getting money from people by threats.

Their victims were mostly ordinary people in their own communities: shopkeepers, workers and families. Governments fought back. In Singapore, colonial law banned secret societies in 1890. Police in Hong Kong and other cities worked against the gangs for many years. Shopkeepers who refused to pay, or who spoke up, took real risks.

Historians use careful words here. Modern triads are descended from the Heaven and Earth Society, not identical to it. The Hongmen split into many groups. Some became political, some stayed fraternal and some became criminal. Most Chinese people, at home and abroad, never had anything to do with triads.

words.d: criminal gangs that trace their roots to the Hongmen; named for a triangle symbol
getting money from people by threats

lessons.title: Tongs: Help First
lessons.mainIdea: Most Chinese American associations, including many tongs, began to help members in a country that shut them out.
reading: In 1882, the United States passed the Chinese Exclusion Act. It barred most new Chinese workers from entering the country. Chinese immigrants already here faced unfair laws and violence. Many could not get help from courts, banks or city officials. So they built their own *associations*, organized groups that serve their members.

Some associations were based on family names or home districts. Others were called *tongs*, from a Chinese word meaning hall or meeting place. They helped members find jobs, settle disputes, get legal help and give the dead a proper burial. A few tongs also ran gambling. In New York in the early 1900s, rival tongs fought violent tong wars. Neighbors who had no part in them often suffered.

Chicago has its own story. In 1926 and 1927, the On Leong Merchants Association built a grand hall at 2216 South Wentworth Avenue in Chinatown. It served as a meeting place for the community. In 1988, federal agents and Chicago police raided an illegal casino inside. The government took the building. In 1993 a church bought it, and since 1994 it has been the Pui Tak Center, a community center. Most people in Chinatown were never part of any crime.

words.d: organized groups that serve their members
Chinese American associations, named for a word meaning hall; most began for mutual aid

look.title: A Chicago Landmark
look.text: The City of Chicago named the former On Leong Merchants Association Building, at 2216 South Wentworth Avenue, a Chicago Landmark on December 1, 1993. The architects Michaelsen and Rognstad designed it, and it was built in 1926 and 1927.

look.prompt: Why might a city protect this building? What stories does it hold besides the 1988 raid?

check.q: What did the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 do?
choices: It created the Heaven and Earth Society
It made Chicago's Chinatown a landmark
It barred most new Chinese workers from entering the United States
It gave Chinese immigrants the right to vote
check.why: The 1882 law shut out most new Chinese workers, one reason immigrants built their own associations.

check.q: What does the word tong mean?
choices: Leopard
Heaven and Earth
Hall or meeting place
Brother
check.why: The reading says tong comes from a Chinese word meaning hall or meeting place.

check.q: What is the former On Leong building in Chicago today?
choices: An illegal casino
A museum of Qing weapons
The Pui Tak Center, a community center run by a church
A triad headquarters
check.why: A church bought it in 1993, and since 1994 it has been the Pui Tak Center.

review.q: When do Qing records show the Heaven and Earth Society began?
choices: Around 1761 or 1762
review.why: Murray and Qin found no evidence before about 1761; 1674 is the legend's date.

review.q: What was the main purpose of the early society, according to Murray, Qin and Ownby?
choices: Mutual aid and protection for poor, traveling men
Overthrowing the Qing from the first day
Running gambling halls
Studying Freemasonry
review.why: These historians argue the society began mainly for mutual aid; political slogans came later.

review.q: How did Qing officials first learn much about the society?
choices: By reading Schlegel's book
By joining it in Honolulu
By questioning members after the Lin Shuangwen uprising in Taiwan
By visiting the Shaolin Temple
review.why: After the 1786 ban and the 1787 to 1788 uprising, officials questioned members and traced the society to Fujian.

review.q: Which is the best description of the Shaolin monks story?
choices: A proven fact from Qing archives
A founding legend members valued, which records do not support
A police report from 1787
A story invented by Chicago newspapers
review.why: The story is the society's own legend; no record from the 1670s mentions it.

review.q: Why was Schlegel's 1866 book useful to colonial governments?
choices: It listed members' home addresses in Chicago
It explained the society's papers, signs and oaths
It proved the society was Masonic
It was written by the Qing emperor
review.why: Schlegel translated seized papers, which helped Dutch and British officials police the society.

review.q: Which statement follows the chapter's careful wording?
choices: Some triad gangs descend from the Hongmen, which also had political and mutual-aid branches
All Chinese associations were gangs
Tongs were founded by Shaolin monks
Triads and the Hongmen are identical
review.why: The chapter says triads descend from the society but are not the same, and the Hongmen split into many kinds of groups.

review.q: Why did Chinese immigrants in the United States build their own associations?
choices: The Qing emperor ordered them to
Unfair laws and officials often shut them out of help
They wanted to copy Ekpe
Schlegel asked them to
review.why: After the 1882 Exclusion Act, many could not get help from courts, banks or officials.

review.q: Which pair shows two different paths Hongmen groups took?
choices: Sande masks and Poro schools
Sun Yat-sen's revolutionary politics and some criminal triad gangs
Nsibidi signs and Abakuá lodges
The Ming dynasty and the Qing dynasty
review.why: Some Hongmen groups turned to politics, as Sun Yat-sen did, while others became criminal triads.
